MR. BLACKBURN-CONTRADICTION BETWEEN REPLY TO WRITTEN QUESTION AND STATISTICS CANADA REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It was only yesterday late in the afternoon that I received in my office a copy of the annual report by the "Dominion Bureau of Statistics" for the fiscal year 1969-70, dated "November 1971."
That report contains a statement concerning the job vacancy survey which is being carried out by Statistics Canada for the Department of Manpower and Immigration. That statement is at substantive variance with the reply given on October 18 of this year by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Jerome) to question No. 1,719 which I had put on the order paper on September 20 of this year.
To my question, "what is the first month in which results from the survey were prepared", the parliamentary secretary replied:	"June, 1970." The Statistics
Canada annual report, page 24, states:
The complete system of this twice-a-month survey, including all mail and field interview phases, became operational late in 1969. Since that time, data have been produced for the Department of Manpower on a regular schedule.
The parliamentary secretary's reply also states that the initial publication will be for the period commencing June, 1970, that thereafter data will be reported monthly and that the initial publication is scheduled to begin before the end of 1971.
My question of privilege relates to the fact that as a member of this House I am only permitted to make inquiry of the ministry, pursuant to Standing Order 39(1). The ministry is not obliged to reply. But since the ministry chose to reply I maintain that I have the right to accurate information.
In view of the statement in the annual report by Statistics Canada, addressed to the Minister of Industry. Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), I am faced with contradictory information.
I do not intend to present a motion at this time, but I will resubmit the same question with the hope that the two ministers involved will agree on a mutually acceptable answer.

subsubtopic: LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-STATEMENT ON OPERATION AND CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement on the recently announced local initiatives program. As of yesterday, December 7, a total of 2,752 applications had been received by the regional offices of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Of these 2,247 were from private groups and organizations and 505 were from municipalities.
The first approvals were made on Wednesday, November 24, and as of yesterday a total of 177 projects had been approved, for a total federal contribution of $4,569,419. It is expected that 2,231 jobs will be created by these projects, all of which are either under way or ready to commence immediately.
Representations have been made by and on behalf of many small communities, indicating that the minimum project size of 30 man-months employment placed the program beyond their capabilities. In response to these representations I am pleased to inform hon. members that the minimum is now reduced to 15 man-months.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our party I want to express our appreciation to the minister for his attention to our observations on the local initiatives program. I want to say as well that we are pleased that our recommendation that the 30 man-month restriction be eliminated was accepted in part but we are still not totally satisfied with the 15 man-month restriction. I firmly believe that this will limit the number of communities that can apply for assistance under the program.
Before making in two or three minutes a few recommendations to the minister, I should like to remind him of some realities that the government must consider in respect of the program. One is that, according to yesterday's figures, 503,000 Canadians are unemployed. Another is the deepening disparities across Canada made evident by the figures released yesterday. This will be further strengthened by argument from other members on motions later. There is also the fact that the program did not officially get under way until November 24 when the first jobs were created and will be terminated in May. The program was not well prepared; it was pulled out of the desks of deputy ministers when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) realized that unemployment was going to be as bad as we had said it would be if no action were taken.
The final reality is that, using the minister's corrected figures given a few moments ago, 231 applications have been approved for 3,000 jobs out of, I would presume, roughly 3,000 applications received. According to the earlier figures the minister gave us, 177 applications had been accepted out of 2,752 received, for the creation of 2,231 jobs. Inasmuch as in the previous month we lost 100,000 jobs in Canada, this does not provide too much consolation to the government or to the people.

Here are a few suggestions for the minister. First, the decision-making process must be speeded up. We have received complaints of applications lodged for 21 days without a response despite the fact that I know that officials in the department are working many hours of overtime to try to accommodate the program. Second, since only 3,000 jobs have been created, and in view of the terrible ratio between applications accepted and applications received, consideration must be given to increasing the funds available. Third, consideration must be given to extending the program beyond the month of May because, as we saw last winter, some of the months with the highest unemployment were in the late spring, even including June. I think the minister must reconsider his position on that particular point. Fourth, consideration must be given to introducing more flexibility into the program in order to allow smaller communities that are not formally, structured as municipalities, local improvement boards or the

I say that because some of these smaller Canadian communities suffer from the highest unemployment rates. Fifth, we believe that special consideration has to be given to areas of high unemployment. I am not referring necessarily to provinces with high unemployment as much as to particular parts of Canada, to certain municipalities or communities that are being hit so hard by the unemployment which has been induced in recent years as a result of the government's restrictive measures. I am especially thinking of the pulp and paper communities across this country that are being devastated as a result of lay-offs.

I should like to join in welcoming the announcement by the minister that the minimum project size under the local initiatives program has been reduced from 30-man months of employment to 15-man months and that applications by or on behalf of educational institutions and hospitals will be considered on their merits and given support under the local initiatives program, where appropriate, when viewed in relation to available funds and other applications from the area. The protests which were received from the provincial governments necessitated further delays and consideration before the plan could come into effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a good thing for the minister to report to the House once in a while on progress made to this day under the local initiatives program.
Personally, I am not at all surprised by the changes that have been made in order to allow a greater number of municipalities or small communities to meet the requirements which, in my opinion, was extremely difficult for some localities to do before. I was precisely telling the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Prud'homme) yesterday that I was worried because the minimum of 30 man-months of work prevented many small rural municipalities from taking advantage of the program. The fact that it has been reduced to 15 man-months should enable a greater number of small municipalities to benefit from the pro-gramm in submitting projects which I hope would be considered acceptable.
What surprises me in all that is that on page 2 of the statement appears the following:
It is now apparent that more applications which meet the basic criteria will be received than can be approved within available funds.
Once more, we have a ceiling because of lack of funds, artificial scarcity of money. Men are available, waiting for work, seeking jobs. Materials are plentiful, dealers and manufacturers are falling all over themselves to sell them. Nevertheless, we shall have to restrict work for lack of funds. An artificial scarcity of money.
I don't know when it will be realized that money should be man's servant and not his master, and that a responsible government in a democratic country such as ours should act as a wise administrator and arrange for money to be available when people plan to carry out work that will benefit the population. In any event, I believe we should consider this matter more thoroughly and take the necessary steps in order that the funds be made available at the proper time, so that we may be able to answer favourably all reasonable requests.
Secondly, I wish to express my sales fact on and congratulate the minister for having amended the program so that school boards and hospital authorities will benefit from it.
Personally, I think it is an improvement from which several Quebec communities and school boards will benefit-I refer to these because I know them best-thus clearing the way for school renovation while creating a number of jobs in appropriate conditions of, instead of cutting branches in four feet of snow workers can do some painting in public building, which the whole community could benefit from, I think this would be a good step forward.

Mr. Speaker, I must limit my remarks because you remind us of it quite often. In concluding, I would simply ask the minister to continue to provide us with information. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask unanimous consent of the House to move a motion under Standing Order 43. I do so because of the November unemployment figures released yesterday by Statistics Canada which showed that the number of unemployed persons in the four Atlantic provinces is 9,000 higher than in the previous month of October.
The unadjusted unemployment rate for each province was greater than in the previous month. In Newfoundland the rate jumped two percentage points to 11.4 per cent. In Prince Edward Island the rate jumped by 2.5 per cent to 7.5 per cent. In Nova Scotia the rate rose from 6.1 per cent to 7.4 per cent, and in New Brunswick the rate increased to 6.5 per cent from 5.5 per cent for the previous month.
In view of this deteriorating situation and the failure of the government's regional economic policies in relation thereto, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald):
That the first report of the Atlantic Development Council, containing recommendations for a development strategy for the region, be referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask leave of the House to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Yesterday in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates the Minister of Manpower and Immigration admitted that $2,220,000 in over-expenditure reflected money spent or to be spent on advertising the local initiative program, the student summer employment program and the Keep Canada Growing campaign. The additional funds represent a 271 per cent increase over the amount originally requested for advertising by the department in the main estimates.
The urgency and importance of this matter are related to the need to ensure beyond all doubt that public funds are not being used, even indirectly, for partisan or electoral purposes, and are also related to the fact that there will be no further opportunity to discuss the matter in the House. I therefore ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson): That the extent and nature of government advertising be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for consideration and report.

speechtext: Did the CBC have some of their equipment stolen in October, 1971 from a parked vehicle in Toronto and, if so (a) what was stolen and what was the original cost of the equipment (b) was the vehicle locked (c) how long had the vehicle been parked in that location (d) on what date was the theft reported and to whom (e) what disciplinary action was taken (f) was the equipment insured and, if so, was the cost of the equipment recovered?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CBC-LOSS OF EQUIPMENT FROM PARKED VEHICLE IN TORONTO
speechtext:
I am
informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: The CBC has no knowledge of any of its equipment being stolen from a parked vehicle in Toronto during October. However, the question probably refers to a missing camera package and its subsequent return in the month of September. The equipment involved was an assembled camera package consisting of an electronic camera, viewfinder, zoom lens and camera shoulder-mount, having a replacement value of approximately $20,000. The CBC truck containing this equipment had been parked on CBC premises and locked at about 11:30 p.m. on September 6 but was found unlocked on the morning of September 9. The theft was reported to the police late that afternoon following internal investigation. No disciplinary action was taken as no case could be established. The equipment, which was insured, was found and returned to the CBC in good working order; hence no claim was necessary.

capital gains taxation applying to farmers. I think almost everybody in this House agrees that if there is to be a reasonable and equitable tax on capital gains, there must be associated with that a significant adjustment in connection with estate taxes and succession duties.
As far as this bill is concerned, the government is simply abandoning the estate tax field. It is suggested that the abandonment of the estate tax field by the federal government solves the whole problem, but it does not. According to my understanding, there has been absolutely no accord reached with the provinces as to what they will do in the field of succession duties. It is all very well for the Minister of Finance and the government to take the attitude that the whole problem will be solved by simply withdrawing from the estate tax field. However, the fact remains that the citizen is the same citizen whether he is caught by a federal estate tax or a provincial succession duty tax.
We are being asked to pass this bill. In fact, it is being forced through the House. The bill involves taxation of capital gains with no assurance as to what the end result will be. With the knowledge we now have, we are likely to end up in a tax jungle with this House being forced to adopt a tax on capital gains, and provincial succession duties piled upon us in a manner which we have no way of knowing will be equitable or in line with the views of a committee of the House of Commons when it was considering this subject. The sensible course would be to defer the capital gains until arrangements have been worked out with the provinces.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In the meantime we should retain the federal estate tax until these arrangements have been made. That is one problem, the relationship with the provinces and the matter of provincial taxation. The second question is, how relevant is this bill to Canada's economic conditions as they exist in the context of the situation that developed over the summer?
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If it was relevant last spring-and this is by no means obvious-it is by no means clear that it is relevant now in the context in which this country finds itself as a result of President Nixon's initiative. We have the DISC proposal in Washington, although the Prime Minister did not feel it necessary to raise this matter with the President. This can have far reaching effects upon Canada. In addition, we have recently been reminded by the Economic Council of Canada of the challenge facing the government and this country in connection with additional jobs and further employment. There is not anything at all cheerful in the recent reports on unemployment published by Statistics Canada.
The need for an industrial development strategy and an economic development strategy in this country has been talked about for years. It was even assumed by the authors of the leaked, so-called Gray report that the government would produce a strategy for economic development and the screening process would be related to implementing that economic strategy. We are being asked to

December 8, 1971
Income Tax Act
adopt this tremendous, complicated morass of legislation with no idea of what the strategy for economic development in this country is going to be.
With regard to the loss of revenue involved, I would hazard a guess that if the estate tax was left in operation it would produce more revenue for the government in 1972 than the capital gains tax proposed in the bill. I agree that what I am proposing will involve some uncertainty in the business world and among taxpayers as to what will eventually be worked out and adopted as a long-range tax plan for this country. However, there is uncertainty anyway. The passage of the bill at this time will not remove the uncertainty that exists. There will be uncertainty, in any event, for many months as far as taxpayers are concerned with regard to getting interpretation on this very complex bill and officials of the Department of National Revenue trying to figure out what it means. There will be these uncertainties plus rulings, and the action taken by the provinces in the field of succession duties. There is a possibility of confusion as a result of the action the provinces may take in the field of personal and corporate income taxes. Passing this bill now will not eliminate these uncertainties.
It will be far better to delay the proclamation of the complex and involved parts of the bill for a while, than to stick the Canadian people and the Canadian economy with these 707 pages of legislation and all the amendments associated with it. The amendment I will propose will provide desirable, uncontroversial and clearly understood parts of this bill relating to personal income taxes coming into effect promptly, with the rest of the bill not being proclaimed until there has been further discussion and an affirmative resolution adopted by this House. I suggest that is the most sensible course to follow.
The reason for the government using closure to jam the bill through at this time is not to aid the Canadian taxpayer and to invigorate the Canadian economy; it is simply the result of stubbornness and a desire to save face. If the government really wants to do something for the economy it should accept the proposition I am putting forward, give priority to the tax reductions that are proposed and inform us of its policies so that we can deal with the serious trade situation that could develop into a crisis if we are not active and careful.
Let the government give us its trade policies. Let it give us its measures to offset the effect of the proposed DISC program in the United States. The government should inform us of its policies for restoring confidence and getting industrial development moving forward at a satisfactory rate, rather than giving us the dismal figures as to expectations as a result of surveys made by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. We do not need bad, ill-conceived bills such as this that do not offer anything to the Canadian people except confusion piled on confusion.
Nothing can undo the mistakes which the government has already made. You cannot recall time. But perhaps my appeal may help this government to at least partially regain its senses. If I can do that, the efforts of myself and my colleagues will not be completely in vain. For the sake of Canada, I hope this is so. I ask the government to accept the amendment which I now propose. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River:
I Mr. Stanfield.]
That clause 1 of the bill be amended by deleting lines 1 to 3 on page 1 and substituting therefor the following:
"1. Parts I to IIIA and parts V to VII of the Income Tax Act are repealed and the following substituted therefor so as to apply, subject to the said act as hereby amended and to part III of this act, to the 1972 and subsequent taxation years but the said act as hereby amended, excepting thereout those portions thereof containing an arrangement, revision and consolidation of the provisions of the said act as the said act is amended by the application mutatis mutandis of the provisions of sections 6 and 8, subsection 12 of section 20, and sections 62, 63, 109, 110 and 117 of the said act as hereby amended, shall not come into force and have effect as law until a day to be fixed by a proclamation that shall be subject to affirmative resolution of the House of Commons:"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have very serious reservations as to whether I can accept the amendment which the Leader of the Opposition has proposed. I would be pleased to hear from hon. members who would like to assist the Chair on the procedural aspect. It does seem to me at this stage of the proceedings-I make these preliminary observations without in any way indicating to hon. members that I have any firm opinion-that the proposed amendment might involve something more than the committee of the whole has power to do. This appears to be a major amendment which might very well be opposed to the principle of the bill which was agreed to on second reading. However, I make this observation without being committed to a firm view and I invite the assistance of hon. members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We agree that a major step is involved in the amendment which my leader has proposed. But let me put it to Your Honour in this way: there is no other means, no other place available to us. Most bills contain a provision naming the date at which the bill is to come into force. The Interpretation Act provides that if there is no such date mentioned in the bill, the measure shall become law upon receiving royal assent. In clause 9 of the bill before us we read that the act shall become effective in certain ways and for certain purposes as of January 1, 1972.
Surely, it is only in committee of the whole that it is possible to deal with a specific clause. Your Honour would agree, I am confident, that it would be absolutely impossible for us to move an amendment of this kind on third reading or to have moved it on second reading. It is true we might on third reading move that the bill be referred back to the committee so the committee might consider certain matters and recommend to the House that parts of the bill be not implemented until a certain time. But if we cannot do so now, when should such an amendment be moved?
It might be argued that we should wait until this debate is finisned. But having regard to the drastic restrictions which have been placed on these discussions-I could use other words but they would not be parliamentary-we shall probably never get to a serious consideration of the balance of the legislation. There are probably 200 sections of this bill which we shall never be able to debate before the guillotine falls. This being the case, my hon. friend has to make a move at this point or not at all.
It should not come as any surprise, because notice was given by way of a speech which my hon. friend made
December 8, 1971

some time ago and in which he declared his intention of moving an amendment of this sort. I believe he said at that time that he would move it with respect to clause 9. Obviously, our prospects of getting to clause 9 are somewhat remote, so if the amendment is to be moved, it must be moved now. In these circumstances, the amendment can only be directed to one clause of the bill, and we are now on clause 1. I submit that an amendment can be moved which has the effect of providing that certain parts of the bill shall come into force at one time and other parts at another time.
If there is a ruling from the Chair that the amendment is not acceptable, I say with all respect there is no other place where it can effectively be moved during the time available for the consideration of this bill. We take this matter very seriously. This is not a spontaneous motion but one with regard to which notice has been given in statements made both inside and outside the House. This is our view of what constitutes a reasonable disposition of the difficulties which confront this country and the House, and only in this way can we place it before the committee.

I would refer Your Honour to the wording of clause 1. These are the operative words bringing about the repeal of the totality of the present Income Tax Act. The 500 or more pages which follow are merely a substitution therefor. If the present act is to be repealed, it must be done at this point. It cannot be done at any other point. The motion put forward by the Leader of the Opposition seeks to repeal certain parts of the act and substitute certain other provisions which include the tax cuts he has enumerated. My hon. friend proposes that the rest can only be proclaimed at a date to be fixed by proclamation, which would be subject to further discussion in the House.
The reasons in support of such a course have been outlined and I would suggest that this is the appropriate place at which to move such a motion, unless Your Honour holds that third reading is the only stage at which this can be done and that there must be a referral back to this committee with instructions to do precisely what Your Honour would forbid the committee to do now.
One has to realize that this is the point of departure. This is the time at which such an amendment must be put. If we are to be told that it must be done on third reading, that there must be a motion to refer back to the committee, should such a motion carry we would be back discussing the same kind of motion as we have just heard this afternoon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: With the same objection.

Yes, with the same objection. We would be back at third reading, and what sort of merry-go-round would that be? I put it to you, Mr. Chairman, that now is the time to put such an amendment, right on clause 1.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If there are no other hon. members who want to assist the Chair on the procedural aspect, since the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Peace River, the hon. member for Edmonton West and others
Income Tax Act
have indicated that they view this amendment very seriously I must say, quite frankly, that I should like a little time to consider it. I would not be fair to the Leader of the Opposition or to other hon. members if I tried to give a decision before satisfying myself about it. If I have the permission of the committee, I should like to take the matter under advisement. I will, of course, make a ruling as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is Your Honour suggesting that we debate the amendment while it is being taken under advisement, or is Your Honour suggesting that we adjourn for that period? The amendment is a very general one in the sense that it does not inhibit general debate. My own view, which I am sure is shared by the mover and by other members of our party, is that we should continue to debate the amendment as if it were in order and had been properly put. Your Honour could then consider your position on the amendment while debate continued.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I first take exception to the suggestion that we adjourn. After all, within two hours from now the entire discussion in committee of the whole will end. That is short enough time, so let us not shorten it any further.
The other comment I wish to make arises out of the fact that we are under an order to end this stage of the debate at 5:45 p.m. Therefore, it seems to me that to have discussion now on a motion which has not yet been accepted, a discussion that might last the full two hours, is unfair to some of us and to others who have proposals they would like to put before the committee. It is very clear that we cannot have all the discussion that we might want before the order becomes operative at 5:45 p.m.; but surely, just as the Leader of the Opposition has had an opportunity to put his amendment, I submit other hon. members should have a similar opportunity to put other amendments.
I think Your Honour should consider that you have called clause 1 and let such members as get the floor make any amendment they may wish to make. Then at some time before a quarter to six Your Honour can rule on the amendment now before the committee, and then at a quarter to six we can vote on all the amendments that are in order. I support the idea of Your Honour having time to consider this amendment, but I think that the rest of us should also have an opportunity to put amendments before the guillotine falls.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that there may be some very fine and meaningful amendments coming from hon. friends to my left, and we are always interested in such amendments. But we think that the amendment that has been moved is a major one, and while I do not want to inhibit my hon. friends I think we should have an opportunity to debate it. It may well be that we are persuasive enough to have the government first bring the Minister of Finance into the committee and then, having brought him in where he can listen to our arguments, be able to convince him that what we have suggested is reasonable. Both of these would be major accomplishments and I do not know whether either of them will take place; but I would not like to see the motion left so there is no opportunity to debate it.
In my view we should debate the amendment now. I do not think that the matter will take very long. It is a simple

amendment and a decision can be made on it if Your Honour holds that it is in order. I think our debate on the amendment should commence now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Peace River was quite correct in assuming that in part I was speaking for myself and my colleagues in suggesting that we have other amendments to move. But I also know that my hon. friends in the Social Credit party have been waiting for days on end for a chance to move an amendment to section 8, which is one of the sections within clause 1. I do not think it would be fair if the remaining 105 minutes were used to debate one subject only when there are other subjects that hon. members would like to put before the committee in time for them to be put to a vote.
The Leader of the Opposition has achieved his main purpose: he has presented this amendment. The next hurdle is to get Your Honour to accept it. Then the final hurdle, of course, is to get it voted on at a quarter to six. However, surely other members should have the same opportunity to move amendments.

Mr. Chairman, I fear that we are treading on very dangerous ground. There is no question about the importance of the motion moved by the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party, but if the Chair does not take a decision very soon and if we were to consider the motion moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) to the effect that his motion be discussed even it has been ruled out of order, this would mean that the House assumes that we believe the amendment is valid. Mr. Chairman, if this motion were to be considered acceptable after one or two hours of discussion, this would mean that all other members would have lost this time during which they could have moved other amendments.
And, as the previous speaker said, we do hope, by 5:45, to be able to submit an amendment allowing workers to deduct the cost of their equipment and other expenses for income tax purposes. We consider such an amendment to be extremely important and I feel that our arguments in this regard would hold water just as well as those of the Progressive Conservatives in favour of their amendment.
That, Mr. Chairman, is why we hope you will render a ruling as early as possible, to avoid our getting onto a slippery slope which would make us waste time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to amendments being put, but since this party, as it usually does, has taken the proper initiative in moving the amendment I feel we should not be deprived of an opportunity of debating it. It might be that other hon. members will have an opportunity to put their amendments, and we are not trying to inhibit them. But we do feel that there should be an opportunity for us, having moved the amendment, to debate it. I do not know what sort of time Your Honour has in mind before arriving at a decision, but I should like to think that in no later than three-quarters of an hour we should have an opportunity to continue the debate.
In the meantime, other hon. members might speak to any amendments they have, allowing a 20-minute limit in

each case. Then possibly we can come back and debate the amendment that has been put. I understand that the other opposition parties would like to have on the record amendments that will not be chopped off at a quarter to six, and I have no objection to that at all.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think we have reached a happy resolution of what might have been an impasse. If Your Honour assumes that you have called clause 1 of the bill, then your next course is to see speakers in whatever order you choose to call them. If, when members of the Official Opposition are called, they wish to speak to their amendments, they should be allowed to do so. If I wish to speak to some other part of clause 1 and to move an amendment, and if my hon. friend for Lotbiniere or one of his colleagues wishes to do the same, then I think that should be allowed. It seems to me that the suggestion that has come out of the discussion does resolve the situation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
And without any help from the
government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think hon. members have resolved the situation and, without binding my colleague who may take the chair later, I do not see any difficulty. I think we should proceed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am now asking for the floor to take part in the debate, not to continue the discussion on the procedural point.
As hon. members are aware, we are getting to the end of committee of the whole discussion on Bill C-259. I think it is unfortunate that there will be so many sections within clause 1 and so many other clauses of the bill which will not be discussed at all before we are called upon to vote on them.
In addition to all the remaining sections within clause 1 and all the other clauses-about 72 of them, covering 100 pages-there are many amendments which have been moved by the Minister of National Revenue and other ministers, so that we really have a tremendous package to deal with at 5.45. It will be interesting to watch the voting on those questions because there will not even be an opportunity for a question to be asked concerning what the various amendments might mean. This is very unfortunate. This, of course, is one of the reasons we opposed the imposition of closure at this stage. However, I must not use all the time there is in complaining too much about that matter when there are a few things I would particularly like to say.
Clause 1 of the bill which we are now discussing includes, in lines 4, 5, 6, and 7, a pretty general statement. It provides:
An income tax shall be paid as hereinafter required upon the taxable income for each taxation year of every person resident in Canada at any time in the year.
So with those words as an introduction to this 596-page clause it would look as though one could talk about anything that is "hereinafter required." One of the requirements stipulated is the rate of taxation. That is found in some of the other sections in clause 1. We have had discussion about those rates and a vote or two on them. I regret
December 8, 1971

there does not seem to be an opportunity to have a discussion on a related matter, namely, clause 3 of the bill. Clause 3 will not be reached because it is beyond page 596. It has to do with the proposal to abolish the collection of special taxes for old age security either from individuals or from corporations.
I wish we had had a chance to get to that clause so that we could discuss this matter. I mention it now because it seems to me it is related to the general rates of tax that will be imposed upon individuals and corporations. In other words, when that clause comes into effect there will no longer be a special tax, either on individuals or corporations, for old age security. Rather, the money for old age security will be obtained from general taxation. That in itself is a good move, which we welcome. We have long contended that a flat tax with a ceiling on it was regressive in nature, and we believe it is far better that the money to be put into the old age security fund should come out of the general sources of taxation. We believe this to be a more progressive basis than the other tax.
However, there is one point which concerns me. This is the reason I wish we had reached the clause, so that we could have had a statement from the government on it. I hope there will not be a tendency on the part of the government to say that the people of Canada will no longer be paying taxes for their old age security, because the language of clause 3 is clear, that there will not be a direct, earmarked tax but that the' Minister of National Revenue will be asked to estimate each year how much would have been collected if that tax were in effect and recommend that that amount be taken out of general taxation and put into the old age security fund.
I should like to make the assertion that even though the imposition of taxes on individuals and corporations for old age security will not continue, the people of Canada both as individuals and corporations will still be paying taxes that go into the old age security fund and, among other things, that establishes their right to benefits under the Old Age Security Act. I note that although the government is prepared to cancel the direct income tax on individuals and corporations for old age security, it has kept in existence the most regressive tax of all, namely, the 3 per cent sales tax for old age security purposes.
Now, sir, this is ground for discussion. If the minister or someone should get the floor this afternoon and want to comment, I would be glad to listen to any such comment. As I say, I welcome the change but I do not want anyone to come around in a year or two and say that the people of Canada are no longer paying taxes for their old age pensions. They will be paying them all right, but in a different way and, indeed, perhaps in a more progressive way.
Among the many things we would like to have done something about is the question of the capital gains tax. The Leader of the Opposition this afternoon indicated that although he favoured the principle of a capital gains tax, he does not like the form in which it is set out in this bill. May I say that our party's position, which has been made clear a number of times, is that the capital gains tax principle does not go far enough.
We agree with the Leader of the Opposition that special consideration should be given to the application of the capital gains tax to farmers, and my colleague, the hon.
Income Tax Act
member for Regina East, has presented an amendment that would deal with that aspect of the matter if it were passed by the committee at 5.45. But apart from that, it is our view that it is grossly unfair and it is a form of discrimination and inequality to say to the industrial worker who struggles in a factory, or to the professional worker who works at his calling, that all the money he earns is taxable income, but to say to persons who enjoy capital gains that only half of it is income for taxation purposes. We think that anomaly should be corrected.
We are all for the kind of protection farmers have sought and the other improvements which perhaps should be made, but so far as the basic principle is concerned we feel the entire amount of a capital gain, wherever a capital gain is taxable, should be considered as the taxpayer's capital gain. In a moment I should like to present an amendment to that effect. But just as the Minister of National Revenue has presented not one amendment at a time but 50 and 95, and other ministers have done the same, I have two amendments and perhaps I might present both now-I was going to say, in order to avoid the necessity of my getting up again but perhaps I should do it now in case I do not get both amendments in before a quarter to six.
My second amendment has to do with the special exemptions given to periodicals like Time magazine and Reader's Digest. There is a section in this bill which grants them concessions, and we think it ought to be deleted. There is no time for the kind of argument that we would like to develop, and it would not be fair to my friends to the left and to the rest to take more time. Therefore, may I present these two amendments so that, like the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition, they may be put to the committee and voted upon at 5.45 p.m. My first amendment reads:
That Bill C-259 be amended at page 97 by deleting the phrase of" from line 4 and also by deleting the phrase " 1 of" from line 9.
That would be an amendment to section 38 of clause 1. Section 38 is the one which says that the tax on a capital gain is one half of the capital gain. We would like to delete the phrase "I of" so that when a person has a taxable gain as defined elsewhere in the act, the whole amount is taxable income just as is the whole amount in the case of an industrial or professional worker. The other amendment that I wish to present is:
That section 19 as set forth in clause 1 of the said bill be amended by striking out subsection (2) on pages 58 and 59.
That is the part of the bill that would provide certain exemptions for magazines such as Time and Reader's Digest. This is an amendment to section 19 of clause 1. I place these two amendments before you, Mr. Chairman, hoping that these two issues as well as others that are outstanding can be voted upon when we reach that point at 5.45 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the Chair might take these two amendments under advisement in order to consider them. I maintain that both amendments are out of order in that both tend to increase taxes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: While it was the intention of the Chair to suggest to the committee that the two amendments be taken into consideration, I was trying at the same time to locate them. I found one, but as to the other I have only an indication of the pages involved. I think the best procedure would be to take a moment to examine the implications of the amendments that have been put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am sure hon. members will wish to co-operate with the Chair in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to support the proposals made a few weeks ago on section 8 by the hon. members who spoke before me. The publicity surrounding this bill and alleging that we were faced with a tax reform entails a thorough consideration of this section and its effects.
It is obvious that this legislation provides for tax deductions, but it is not certain that these changes are really valid. I, for one, think that the advantages of the legislation are very limited as compared with its disadvantages.
For example, when we see that the legislation in force as well as the bill under consideration recognize the right of contractors, salesmen, lawyers and doctors, to deduct the cost of their machinery, equipment or other expenses incurred in the exercise of their activities, whilst the government proposes to limit the amount deductible by workers to $150 per year or 3 per cent of their income whichever is the lesser, we maintain that there is an anomaly somewhere.
The only obvious conclusion which we can draw is that lumberjacks, mechanics and construction workers, for example, have been discriminated against and, in short, there is a flagrant injustice towards the majority of Canadian workers.
I acknowledge that the amount of $150 would cover part of the expenses incurred by some workers, but these are very few. In fact, it is not an amount which is granted to the workers, since its deduction is allowed. Actually, it represents some $20 to $25 per year.
Mr. Chairman, if this is not a mockery of the worker and his efforts, I wonder how we can describe this attitude. The minister has probably not thought of it, which is normal when one considers how busy he is. It is also possible that the officials who drafted the bill are spoiled kids who have entered the public service because of the protection they enjoyed, guys who think that they know it all and do not realize that other citizens contribute to the progress of this country and to the increase in Canadian production.
I think it is quite possible that those officials who have never seen anything but the streets of Ottawa and the beaches of Florida might have forgotten the working classes. This is why I say that an allowance of $150 per year is not much for the employee of the forest industry who has to drive 40 to 50 miles a day to and from his work. The $150 allowance does not even cover half the cost of registration of the car or small truck he could not do without.
Mr. Chairman, there are also those who have to drive 50 to 100 miles on the weekend and who must pay transpor-

tation expenses as well as for the purchase and maintenance of chain saws. Again, it is obvious in this case that the $20 tax deduction is far from the actual amount they will have to pay.
Also the construction workers who on top of their travelling expenses must buy equipment that can cost up to $1,000 in certain cases and that needs to be replaced and repaired.
Everybody knows that the workers have to travel more than they ever did. The jobs are less and less permanent. Sometimes a great number of workers have to travel in order to follow their bosses. Contractors from Trois-Rivieres get contracts in Quebec City and bring workers there who must travel every weekend. Contractors from all areas get contracts outside of their territory and if the workers want to keep their jobs they myst follow their boss and often pay the costs.
Mr. Chairman, for a Parliament member earning $26,000 per year, public accounts for the year 1970 show expense accounts of $4,000, $5,000 and even $6,000. A member who lives near Parliament has a smaller account, another who lives farther a bigger one. Everybody agrees with that. I repeat: It is strange indeed that in the case of a worker earning only $6,000 or $7,000 per year, Bill C-259 should provide for a deduction of $150 only, while in the case of a member earning $26,000, the deduction for expenses may amount to $6,000.
Mr. Chairman, this government has been in power for three and a half years and the people have been waiting for three and a half years for the establishment of a just society. I think that certain proposals will have to be taken into consideration if we want to come up with more than $20 a year for the workers' expenses.
As regards mechanics, the implementation of section 8 of Bill C-259 is also discriminatory if we compare it with the method applied for dentists, doctors and all other professionals.
It is ridiculous to offer a $150 deduction per year to mechanics.
We all have friends who are mechanics. Everybody knows that the mechanic who has to buy a complete set of tools must pay $1,400 or $1,500 for it. We also know that some tools must be replaced and in spite of depreciation the value of those tools is always between $1,200 and $1,500.
I am entirely in favour of permitting doctors, lawyers and other professionals to deduct the cost of replacement of their equipment as well as other expenses incurred in the discharge of their duties. However, I am convinced that the same treatment should be granted workers in the fields of forestry, construction and automobile.
The government allows substantial deductions to groups of persons who complete their tax returns according to their conscience. When it comes to taxation, however, some people slip their conscience into their pocket, under their handkerchief.
Mr. Chairman, whenever I consult my lawyer and obtain some advice allowing me to do good business, I am satisfied. I am ready to give him $15 or $20.1 pay cash and
December 8, 1971

do not ask for a receipt. And when my wife and other members of my family go to the dentist, the same thing happens.
If my son or my daughter has a toothache, I spend $10 to help him or her sleep soundly and the whole family is happy. The deal is good, the $10 bill is handed over and no receipt is asked for.
Indeed the government does not know how much these people earn each year; nonetheless, it acknowledges all their expenses. Today, by proposing an across-the-board amount of $150 as employment expenses for the worker, the government recognizes that there is discrimination between wage-earners and professionals. Finally the government has recognized the existence of a problem and has tried to do something about it. Unfortunately, it has followed its usual bureaucratic method and has adopted a standard exemption, casting everybody in the same mould. The same exemption will be allowed to the employee who needs only a bail-point pen while certain workers in the building industry must buy $500 to $1,000 worth of tools.
I think it is an appropriate opportunity for the government to decide to eliminate this inequity already tolerated for too long. This inequity is recognized but still no concern is shown for the work-man who invariably comes last.
I wonder for how many years we will have to protest in the House and outside so that justice prevail and laws be identical for all taxpayers. When shall we stop passing special laws? In the case of the auto workers, when the owner of a repair shop buys the very same tools he is allowed to deduct the depreciation from his income along with the cost of replacing and repairing them while the workman is imposed a $150 limit or 3 per cent of his income, whichever is the lesser.
Mr. Chairman, the remarks I am making today are based on experience since I worked as a lumberjack and a carpenter before my two years as manager of a company in the building trade. I have witnessed hundreds of those inequities, always at the workman's disadvantage.
It will be argued that by allowing the workers to deduct expenses incurred in their trade, the application of the legislation would be difficult and costly, but I consider this a very weak argument. We could ask ourselves why its application would be more difficult for workers than for professionals. I believe its implementation is easier for workers than for professionals.
In the case of wage earners, the department knows exactly how much they make, while it does not even know the income of professionals or others. Very often, expenses that are in no way related to the nature of the business are claimed by the taxpayer as deductions.
Mr. Chairman, it would be interesting to find out how many wives of professionals, industrialists, merchants have the advantage of using a car whose depreciation costs are claimed by the business or businesses the husband owns. How many expenses are deducted for business trips which are in fact only pleasure trips! I could go on giving similar instances for a long time.
Mr. Speaker, we should return to facts and stop being so stingy with workers. We have been hearing about a thor-
Income Tax Act
ough fiscal reform, but now is the time, I feel, to make a thorough job of it so that the law may be the same for all.
Therefore, I move, supported by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That section 8(1) of clause 1 be amended by substituting, in line 25, the word "all" for the words "such of", by deleting the word "following" in line 26 and by adding after the word "source", in line 27, the words "with supporting papers".
Mr. Chairman, the adoption of this amendment will allow the Canadian taxpayer to do with his expense account what he does now with receipts for charitable donations. This amendment would make it possible for the taxpayer which has very few expenses to avail himself of the deduction of $150 or of 3 per cent and those who will claim the deduction for greater expenses will be treated according to their tax returns and supporting evidence.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I would like to support the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition. It gives force to the reasons that I expressed earlier this week and several times last week as to why passage of the bill should be deferred. We have gone over this time and time again. I want to add a further reason which has to do particularly with hon. members who come from the province of Quebec. This refers to the result of the elimination of the estate tax.

I am told by representatives of the Society of Notaries that practically every will which includes the term "subject to the federal law" will have to be changed and that they do not know in what sense precisely. In the same way, if a will contains the term "subject to the provincial law" changes will have to be made and, again, they do not know in what way. Until there is agreement between the federal government and each province as to the impact of its succession duty, it is merely compounding confusion to insist upon passing this bill and its provisions dealing with repeal of the estate tax. The federal government has no right to tell the provinces to conform, but that is precisely what the provision we will vote on today is telling them- "Come to heel or else you will be responsible for any mess".
The provinces have equal jurisdiction with the federal government, but the federal government is insisting that the law come into effect on January 1. I say it has no more right to do this than has the province of Ontario to insist that the government of Canada amend the law to conform with theirs. They have the right to levy personal and corporate taxes. The provinces have rights with regard to the levying of succession duties, but by agreement only which expires in 1972. The federal government has offered to collect this income tax based on a uniform tax law in the provinces, and eight provinces have agreed. Ontario has farmed out the collection of personal income tax to the federal government but collects its own corporate tax.
The province of Quebec collects its own personal income tax and corporate income tax. Ontario collects its own succession duties, as does the province of Quebec. British Columbia has moved into the field of succession duties, 75 per cent, and all the other provinces which have a succession duty can get 75 per cent of the proceeds of estate tax under redistribution by agreement and they do not levy their succession duties. That is the way to get accord.
Mr. Chairman, today this government is asking members to tell the provinces, "We don't care a hoot about you. Come to heel and conform to this act". Most of the corporations of Canada are located in Ontario and Quebec, but neither province is in a position to amend its Corporation Tax Act nor to conform with this act. Of course, they may not want to amend and they have a perfect right not to. In this time of economic difficulty all we get are cracklings from the Prime Minister and other ministers to the effect that they are doing all they can to help the economy recover. But it is a backdoor approach. If any hon. member feels that he has greater wisdom than members on this side, let him undertake to operate a corporation in Ontario or Quebec as successfully as it should be operated.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I will take that on.

With two tax systems that operate on different principles? I invite the Minister of Transport to operate them as successfully as it should be done, under two separate systems of taxation and even fundamental differences in principle. If the minister thinks that the office of Minister of Transport is some-

times difficult, I suggest that he would go straight up the wall and through the roof as a result of trying to operate such a business. Yet this is what the government is compelling businessmen in Ontario and Quebec to do. I wonder at the gall, the unmitigated arrogance displayed in that attitude. It is not just a question of trying to override the opposition because they have greater muscle. Just who do they think they are trying to overcome?
Mr. Chairman, those idle cracklings that come out of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre-
We have heard this speech ten times.
Sometimes in order to get through a thick skull one has to repeat, and I am telling the Minister of Agriculture, who in fact has one of the thickest skulls in this House-

Shame!

I have made my point. We have repeated this argument. The facts are there, and the people will remember. The other day I brought forward an amendment to section 3 with regard to the capital gains tax affecting farmlands. At that time, for purposes of greater clarity and certainty, I ought to have brought forward a companion amendment to section 39. Therefore, to make sure that there is consistency in the stand that we have taken on section 3 with regard to farmlands disposed of for continuing farming purposes, I wish to move an amendment to section 39 as follows:
That section 39 of clause 1 be amended by:

and substituting therefor the word "or" and

(iv) land used in farming as defined in this act and to be used for continuing farming and

It is difficult to draft these amendments because the original provision is extremely complex. However, I think the purport of the amendment is clear.
My third point is this. The other night we embarked on an extensive discussion on section 239(2) which deals with the indictment procedure. That procedure may be invoked at the election of the Attorney General of Canada. Since the government's position needs clarifying, I have moved an amendment. That amendment, in this case to section 235, says that there shall not be a penalty under any regulation that is made retroactively under section 221(2). In case the Minister of Justice wishes clarification, let me say that section 221(2) provides that a regulation shall not be effective until it shall have been published in the Canada Gazette, but if it is so stated in the regulations it can have a retroactive effect prior to the date of publication. I do not want there to be a penalty with regard to the period between the so-called effective date and the date of publication. There are many things wrong with the principle of having offences created under a regulation that has not been published because it will not be known that such an offence exists. My amendment to section 235 seeks to correct this. I agree that a regulation can have retroactive effect, but I do not agree that there shall be any penalty thereunder.
I should like to know the government's position on section 239(2), bearing in mind the amendment I have moved. I know that certain members of the government expressed reservations, as I did, about the justice of
Income Tax Act
allowing a minister of the Crown, even on the basis of incontrovertible facts put before him by the Minister of National Revenue, to say that a man shall go to jail. Under section 243 the court has no right to suspend sentence. I do not believe that any minister of the Crown has that right. I do not believe that he has the right to decide that a man shall go to jail. It is for the court to decide whether a man shall go to jail and, surely, not for a minister, a deputy minister or a director of prosecutions.
In no circumstances must we have that law in Canada. There can be adequate provision as to the sentence to be imposed by the court, and that shall be subject to appeal. Surely to goodness there should not in these cases be proceedings by way of indictment, especially since the finding of the court may indicate a considerably lesser offence than that charged in the information. For instance, a man may be charged with defrauding the Crown of a quarter of a million dollars and it may turn out that the amount is only $2,000. Yet because of the indictment procedure the man must go to jail. There is no relief; there can be no suspended sentence under section 243. This procedure may be invoked at the election of the Minister of Justice.
I never heard of such nonsense in any bill.
