speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: When I look at this bill I am reminded of the phrase "For whom the bill tolls". It tolls for members opposite, members on this side and all the taxpayers of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: With the reductions!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have been attempting to secure an equitable arrangement so that those parts of the bill which are necessary to provide stimulation of the economy will become law without further delay. The complex and difficult measures which the Minister of Finance and his officials do not understand should await careful deliberation before becoming law. We have the imposition of closure in an even more insidious way. If the member for Hamilton-Wentworth wishes, we can get into a debate on that point. If this were really closure a motion would have to be moved in respect of every section. This is a much more infamous way of dealing with it. We have been deprived of debating these measures. This is why rule 75C was invoked rather than the more moderate closure measure rule which any normal government would have invoked. Because of this closure there is no opportunity for reasonable debate and discussion on many of the sections.
Do hon. members know that we have passed between 115 and 120 sections? There are still over 200 sections and subsections to be passed. There has been casual discussion on them but not the kind of debate which is essential on such an important matter. This infamous conduct on the part of the government makes it all the more necessary to suspend the operation of those parts of the bill to which my leader referred in the speech he made earlier today. Members opposite say that we have had discussion. We want more than discussion, Mr. Chairman; we want discussion leading to change. There are some parts of the bill which do not need change. We admit that. We are reasonable people.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Why did your members not attend the committee?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There are many sections which need change. The proof of that is in the fact that day after day amendments were brought forward by the government. I challenge the genial Minister of Finance to stand in his place now and deny that during the next session the government will be introducing substantial amendments to the Income Tax Act. I am prepared to yield to the minister if he will accept my challenge. His refusal to accept it is proof that what I have said is correct.
I call as a witness one of the minister's colleagues, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. He has a bill before the House in respect of the competition act. He is now engaged in chewing it up piece by piece, trying to explain away the fact that the bill will not be proceeded with in this session. He has made so many speeches that it is hard to keep up with him, but in a speech to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in Montreal on November 30 he said:
We have developed new techniques for the introduction of the legislation, by inviting the co-operation of the people with the
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.)
practical knowledge and experience to make their own studies of the proposals and to put forward their view-
Surely, this is the responsible and appropriate way to approach legislation so fundamental to our economic life as the competition act.
For that I substitute "the amendments to the Income Tax Act."
And an approach consistent with producing sound legislation. To the extent that we can draw on the views of businessmen from the different sectors of the economy-
I think he said something different when the labour people were before him. I think he substituted "labour people" for "businessmen."
-that we are able to understand, and thus take account of, the particular needs of the many diverse and often conflicting elements that make up the Canadian economy-
I know that members opposite say that we have had a lot of discussion. Of course we have, as we must have discussion on matters so intrinsically important as this. We are not now dealing with the original discussion, the white paper or the original royal commission report; we are dealing with a bill which only came into our possession at the beginning of September.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: July 12. You were not here all summer.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I was here throughout most of July. It is necessary to have a watchdog here to keep check on this government. I was here but I did not see this bill until after this session began.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: You need a new secretary.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I have every reason to suspect it was probably leaked to me then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, when I am finished. I have a lot to say and little time in which to say it. That is what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs had to say. It is not the way this bill has been rammed through this House. I suggest to hon. members and to the people of Canada that there is coming shortly a day of retribution. The Minister of Finance, his parliamentary secretary, all the members of the government and their supporters will have to answer to the taxpayers at the polls at the next election. That is the day they fear; that is the day they dread. I suggest that they now give thought to this last opportunity presented by the Leader of the Opposition and support his motion.
Only yesterday the government proposed very substantial amendments with regard to co-operatives and credit unions. The night before, as a result of proposals of this party, the government took into account some very cogent and reasonable arguments we made with regard to the administrative clauses. During the reasonably short debate on this bill, 135 or 140 amendments have been introduced by the government. Surely it is common sense to suspend the operation of these more difficult sections until there has been further opportunity for consideration. How is it possible for the tax experts, lawyers, accountants and their advisers, as well as the advisers of officials and corporations, to competently and intelligently advise their clients, the taxpayers of this country,
December 8, 1971

where they stand? I doubt if many of the ministers' advisers can do so. If so, they have not discharged their function. Certainly the minister and his parliamentary secretary do not understand them as well as they should.
In light of the amendments which have been introduced, and the fact the minister has not denied that he will be introducing a host of amendments in the next session, we have one of two ways in which to look at this matter. Either the government introduced the bill knowing it would be changed, which is both hypocritical and fraudulent-and this government excels in both of those characteristics-or they introduced the bill without being aware of its meaning and effect, which is plain stupid and indicates both administrative and parliamentary incompetence. I do not know on which pan of the scale to lay it. I think that in large measure it consists of both fraudulence and hypocrisy, and stupidity and incompetence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Watch your language.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
When the government introduces amendments on the scale it has done, how can its members have the unmitigated gall to say to the country, "Please pass this bill. We want it through. We want every part of it and we are not prepared to accede to the reasonable request of the Leader of the Opposition." It shatters my faith in the government, what little faith I have left. Talking of shattering, I address this question to the minister: What shattering tragedy would come about if he were to accept the amendment offered by my leader? If it lies within the scope of the mind of man to devise a monstrosity like this bill, the same mind should be able to change it, to adapt it to cover the requirements of the amendment moved by my hon. friend.
There is another aspect. We are aware of the experience in the United Kingdom. Some years ago they introduced there, not a massive bill of the kind before us, one which is well called the "First Book of Ben," but a relatively short bill providing for a capital gains tax. I was in Britain not long ago. I talked with some of the officials there and they told me the measure had given rise to one of the most vexing administrative problems their competent and experienced staff had ever been called upon to face, namely, the integration of the new capital gains tax into the existing tax structure.
However, the government of Canada is not satisfied with this. They are providing for other changes as well. All the preponderance of convenience rests with us with regard to changes we have proposed. I know the answer may well be that any more delay will result in further uncertainty. But how much more uncertainty could there be than the uncertainty which presently perplexes the business community? It will be many months, possibly many years before tax appeal decisions have been handed down on a great many of the point which are now in doubt. I shall be greatly surprised if within a year or two not less than 150 amendments are brought in to change the unworkable and iniquitous provisions of the bill before us.
I conclude by saying this. Taxes, like death, are very final. What we are seeing now is a form of fiscal euthanasia. It is a tax rip-off. It will place small business
Income Tax Act
people, farmers and everybody else in a terrible predicament. I urge the minister to repent at the last minute, to stand up now and say; "I recognize the validity of the arguments which have been made. I respect the views of the Leader of the Opposition and I am prepared to accept his amendment." If he will do this, he will rise very sharply in my esteem. I shall now give the hon. gentleman an opportunity to do so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? He said he did not get a copy of this bill until September. Did he ever write to the Minister of Finance and ask him to deliver one as soon as it was available?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No. I understand there is a distribution office here and when bills are left at the distribution office they are to go to members. The only reason I did not get the bill was that it did not go to the distribution office.
You were not here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If I might have the indulgence of the committee I should like to take a moment or two, in connection with the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition, to deal with the point of procedure which the Chair raised and which was ably argued by hon. members who assisted the Chair.
The Chair is of the opinion that in the circumstances in which we are operating today, that is to say, when an order of the House imposes a time limit upon debate, it would be exceedingly difficult for the Leader of the Opposition to redraft his amendment should it be found that it was necessary to do so in order to meet procedural difficulties which might arise.
I shall not take the time of the committee to deal in detail with a matter which touches on an important constitutional question, but the final words of the motion proposed by the Leader of the Opposition cause me some extra concern. I mention this so there may be no misunderstanding. I refer to the words "shall not come into force and have effect as law until a day to be fixed by a proclamation that shall be subjected to an affirmative resolution of the House of Commons." This seems to propose a new concept in the legislative process. It is very doubtful, to my way of thinking, whether any precedent could be found to support the proposition that an amendment to a financial bill can override the principle that an act passed by two Houses of Parliament cannot be nullified by a resolution of either House. That is fundamental.
Having made this observation, however, I do not consider it to be a question to be summarily dealt with by the Chairman of the committee of the whole at this time because of its important constitutional implications. I do not wish to deal with this aspect for the time being, because of the lack of time this afternoon and the attendant circumstances. In my opinion, the committee should be allowed to resolve the question and I shall accordingly put the amendment. Is it the wish of the committee that I read the amendment again?
Dispense.

I have listened for the last few minutes to my good friend, the hon. member for Peace River. He

December 8, 1971
Income Tax Act
used a few words like "fraudulent" and "hypocritical" and actually applied them to me. Not only was the government guilty of fraud and hypocrisy, he said, but its supporters were fraudulent and hypocritical. That includes me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, no.
May I respectfully point out that people in glass houses should never throw stones?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, I would not for the world be guilty of using the words "fraudulent" and "hypocritical" in relation to members of this House. I said the government was hypocritical and fraudulent or else stupid and guilty of both administrative and parliamentary incompetence. Anyone who wants to extricate an adjective out of the last phrase can do so, but not the first.

I think the hon. member probably said a few things which were not in his notes. However, I am glad to accept his apology. When the Carter commission was picked in 1962, the right hon. member for Prince Albert was meticulous in his choice. The commission was picked by a Tory government. Ever since the Carter commission brought in its report our friends have been running away from it as if it had a very bad case of diptheria. As far as any tax legislation and changes are concerned, since the Carter report there has been at least nine years' gestation, and even an elephant requires only two years. We could have developed a whole herd of elephants in Africa in the time it has taken to bring in tax changes in this country.
There are many good things in this bill. If the government is to be criticized at all, I think the criticism should be levelled at the fact that it is only now that we have taken a firm stand. In June, 1968, the government was picked by the people of Canada to govern. The reason hon. members on the government side are sitting where they are is that the people of Canada had confidence in them.
Hear, hear!

The reason opposition members are sitting where they are, and where they will remain for many years, is that the people have no confidence in them. Some people hum and haw about things for years, but it is high time hon. friends to my left understood that they lost the last election and that the government has a duty to govern. As a backbencher of the Liberal party I am glad the government has finally taken this initiative.
As I say, there are many good things in this bill. I think, for example, of the increased exemptions for all people in Canada. Approximately one million Canadians, once this bill is passed, will no longer pay tax as they have in the past. This is a bill of which we should all be proud. In addition, there are one million old age pensioners in Canada who, through the goodness of this government, are receiving benefits supplementary to the basic old age pension and who will no longer pay tax as a result of the provisions of this bill. I say that the Minister of Finance should stand up and take a bow.
Hear, hear!

For years the mothers of Canada have complained not only to Conservative members but to all Members of Parliament that if they go out to work they have to employ a baby sitter to look after their family. There was no way they could get an exemption for the money thus expended. But now such a proposal is being implemented and I say that the mothers of Canada are proud of the government.
Furthermore, although our Tory friends have talked about implementing the capital gains tax, they are afraid to face the fact that it is only common sense that the man who makes half a million dollars on the stock market should be prepared to pay his just dues to society in the same way as if he is in receipt of a salary. Ninety-eight per cent of the people of Canada are in favour of a capital gains tax. Every western country supports such a tax, and they do so because it is a tax that is just and right. Our Tory friends who are sticking up for business interests do not have the gumption to stand up and say that a capital gains tax is a good thing.
It is true that this is a very large and comprehensive bill. It may also be true that there is no one in Canada who understands the entire bill. But that part of the legislation affecting 99 per cent of the people of Canada is very easy to understand and the people of Canada will appreciate it when it is passed and comes into effect on January 1 next. For too long have we been lead-swinging on the subject of tax legislation in this country. As far as I am concerned, the criticism that can be levelled at the government is that it did not take the initiative several months ago and do what it is now doing. The government was sent here to govern. The time for talk is passed; that is something hon. friends to my left should remember.
Periodically the Tories hold a convention and change their name. I remember when they were the good old Conservative party. Then they became the Progressive Conservative party. In view of the way they are acting on this bill, or were a couple of days ago, they should change their name to the retrogressive Conservative party-looking forward into the past and backward into the future. We need a constructive opposition in this chamber and the government does want to have a few members of the opposition back here after the next election. If the opposition would be a little more responsible, then at least some of them might get back here.
I have elaborated upon only four or five of the many good points in the bill. Lest my Tory friends think we are unwilling to face the electorate on this bill, let me tell them that we are willing to accept the gauntlet whenever the Prime Minister throws it down.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Chairman, in support of the amendment moved by my colleague from Portneuf (Mr. Godin), I believe that this is probably the last opportunity I shall have of speaking during the debate in committee of the whole on Bill C-259, because the government-contrary to the wishes of all opposition parties and consequently of the majority of the Canadian people
Income Tax Act
which they represent-has decided unilaterally to put an end to the debate on a subject that is nevertheless very important since it will affect for many years to come the taxation system applicable to millions of individuals and thousands of corporations.
Once again I say that the party in power is the only one that can assume responsibility for this unfortunate decision, and it will have to attempt to explain to the people of Canada why it has compelled the legislators to vote in a few hours on a great many sections of this bill which are still remaining and some of which are nevertheless most important.
I quite agree on the need for a total tax reform to correct, among other things, some intolerable situations that in many cases had become obvious display of iniquity and frustration.
If I can support without any hesitation many provisions of the bill before us, I must also say that I can't do the same in connection with several others which seems to me completely inappropriate.
Thus, I felt it my duty to fight vigorously the notion of employed capital which was proposed as the main method of computing the co-operatives' taxable income. In this regard, I am very happy that the government has finally agreed to give more flexibility to its initial position and to delete this most controversial aspect.
There is however another point of prime importance which I must discuss. Indeed, I have objected since the beginning to section 8 (1) (a) which limits the employment expenses deductible from earnings from that employment. I really cannot see why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) establishes an arbitrary maximum of 3 per cent or $150. It seems illogical to me not to grant the thousands of taxpayers who use the T-l short income tax return the same rights and privileges from which other classes of taxpayers benefit, including professionals of every category.
I think the government should take account of all the types of workers whose tools and travelling expenses eat up a substantial part of their modest income. Let us take for example a mechanic or a carpenter who, even before beginning to make a profit, must spend several hundred dollars for basic equipment or tools to which will be progressively added some quite costly implements many of which must regularly be replaced.
The same applies to the logger who in addition to being away from his family for weeks must bear heavy travelling expenses and considerable expenses for the purchase, maintenance and replacements of the essential tools of his trade.
As for travelling expenses, it seems to me entirely normal that they be deducted from taxable income, taking into account however such restrictions as a reasonable daily or weekly commuting distance. Let us consider, among others, the thousands of employees of the private and public transportation systems-railways workers, truckers, etc.-who are compelled to eat most of their meals away from home; as a result, they incur additional expenses for food and in some cases also, for lodging, both of which are basic individual needs and therefore lead to unavoidable expenses.
The government should therefore allow, in computing the taxable income, that those additional expenses directly related to such employment be taken into account.

Finally, I shall bring up another case in support of this proposal; the case of miners who, because the closing down of mines operating in an area close to their homes, must henceforth earn their livelihood at locations sometimes pretty far from their main residence, resulting either in major weekly, bi-montly or monthly travelling expenses, added to the expenses of setting up a secondary residence or, alternately, in a decision to move the whole family which involves, over and above disruption of the individuals social environment, the quite substantial material costs of actual moving expenses.
Mr. Chairman, I am not inventing those facts; they are real problems which hundreds of miners must face in Abitibi. We are actually witnessing in this area a constant shift of the Timmins-Rouyn-Noranda-Malartic-Val d'Or mining operations toward new development centres of mining explorations always located more to the north, hence the newly created towns of Matagami, Chibouga-mau and Chapais. These problems of regional economy, which directly affect the mobility of miners, are not only in this outlying Quebec area. I am convinced that other provinces are at grips with this type of difficulties. Those are, of course, very complex problems which the government, unfortunately, seems to overlook in its tax reform legislation.
I therefore ask the Minister of Finance to kindly reconsider seriously section 8(l)(a), that all types of workers might in the future deduct from their taxable income all expenses related directly to their work. The government owes it to itself to meet the needs and aspirations of all Canadian workers, and not only of various groups of professionals who already benefit from the advantages we request. The government cannot, in all honesty, treat individuals differently, according to their social status or occupation. The contribution of every worker, regardless of his trade or occupation, is important to the community and constitutes an essential part, an important fraction of a whole called the "collective effort" of society. It is therefore here and now, more than ever, that the Liberal slogan of the "just society" should be put into practice. The concept of equality of citizens in matters of taxation should also be recognized in the section of the bill dealing with deductions applicable. Otherwise, the general principle of tax equity underlying the bill before us will be defeated.
It is not a question here of claiming rights or privileges for a small group of citizens. It is rather a matter of including a general provision of which all workers could avail themselves and which would affect them more directly.
For instance, according to Statistics Canada, the number of workers in logging in 1969, was estimated at 64,900 and that of construction workers at 377,200. Those are two classes of workers who would benefit from our proposal. Construction workers only represented, in August 1971, about 6.8 per cent of Canada's labour force. If we add all the other groups of workers already mentioned, we find that they represent a very substantial part of the total labour force, which shows the importance of protecting them as much as the other citizens who benefit from a different tax treatment as regards deductions and 
who have nevertheless a substantially higher income than the workers affected by the proposal before us now.
Finally Mr. Chairman, while deploring the insanity of the coercion climate in which the debate on Bill C-259 is to come to a close, I should like to ask all my colleagues who are really concerned about respect for the fiscal equity principle and whom the arguments I stated may have influenced, to support unreservedly the amendment presented today by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin).
This amendment would include in the deductible elements of income all expenses directly related to the work of the individual whose transportation expenses exceed some limit to be set by regulations made under the legislation. We must consider that this amendment could, among other things, grant construction workers, lumbermen and mechanics the right to deduct from their income their various moving expenses and the cost of purchasing, maintaining and replacing their tools.
In the final analysis, such a provision would only bring about a higher degree of justice, since besides the classes of workers abovementioned and which would be the more affected, this proposal could also be applied, it need be, to all the groups of workers in our society who must incur large expenses in the practice of their main trade.
Therefore I believe that all the classes of workers I have mentioned largely contribute to build up and maintain many things that benefit the whole society.
If a husband and father leaves his family for weeks or months to work hundreds of miles away from his home, for instance to supervise the construction of a hospital or take part in the extraction of our natural resources, often in difficult and sometimes inhuman conditions, he deserves the same benefits granted to others able to earn larger sums of money in much better conditions.
After the government introduced amendments to the sections concerning the co-operatives, Caisses populaires and credit unions, several hon. members discovered their call was to defend such institutions, whereas at the start of the debate they were completely mute. This is the time to speak up for the Canadian workers to whom justice is not rendered under Bill C-259. All hon. members who belatedly took position on sections 136 and 137 must now have the courage to support the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants for sharing these last four minutes with me. I indicated that I would like the floor for this short period mainly to indicate how we intend to vote on the amendment proposed this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition. As hon. members are aware, despite any good that is in this bill, and despite the improvements that we have been able to have included in it in the last few days, we still feel there is so much in the bill that is bad that we have no alternative but to vote against it when we reach third reading, as indeed we shall do this evening.
However, Sir, we do not feel that we can support the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition. We take this position for three reasons. In the first place, it seems to us that if the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition means anything, it involves concessions to big business. We do not go along with those concessions. In the second place, we do not think that the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition means anything for big business or for anything else, because if the amendment were carried and written into the bill and the bill were passed in that way, all the taxes in the bill would eventually come into force just as they are now spelled out in the bill and the people who thought they were getting something by the amendment would be fooled. They would not get anything at all except a change in the date when the tax changes would come into effect.
Our third reason for being opposed to the amendment is that we have too much regard for the parliamentary system. We think that trying to pass a bill through both Houses, yet having in it a provisional clause, is not the way to deal with legislation. We are against the bill. We are against this monstrosity. We deplore the fact that we have not had a chance to discuss hundreds of its pages. We deplore what will take place in about 30 seconds from now. But we do not think the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition makes any improvement. Therefore, we shall vote against it.
